speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The quality of human resources is key to boosting investment, innovation, productivity and entrepreneurship in a developed economy like ours.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Effective education is tied to quality of life, and good physical and mental health.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In this speech, I shall argue for smaller form class sizes in Primary and Secondary schools with consequent reductions in the size of all classes conducted.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We should push for improvement on other fronts, like reducing the script marking workload for teachers which my colleague Mr Dennis Tan asked about recently.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But smaller class sizes for core subjects have the potential to unlock many other benefits, especially given the need to grow innovation, productivity and entrepreneurship in an era of artificial intelligence and disruption, where growing non-cognitive skills and attributes are so important.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is not a new subject and has been raised multiple times in this House by current and former Workers' Party Members of Parliament and Non-constituency Members of Parliament, such as Mr Yee Jenn Jong, Mr Png Eng Huat and Assoc Prof Daniel Goh.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is above the norm for other developed countries and also substantially above the norm for the Gifted Education Programme classes, private tuition centre classes and classes for most international schools operating in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Having said that, subject-based banded classes and remedial classes may be smaller, though I was informed in a reply to an earlier Parliamentary Question that the size of remedial classes is not tracked by MOE.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Class size decreased in countries with the largest classes in 2000 whereas it stayed the same or increased slightly in the countries which already had small class sizes in 2000.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Smaller class sizes allow teachers to focus on obtaining more teacher-student interaction during class time.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This achieves several benefits as demonstrated by research.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: A literature review by the US Centre for Public Education based on an analysis of 19 studies showed a positive link, even if there are other factors at play.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I quote, "Some researchers have not found a connection between smaller classes and higher student achievement, but most of the research shows that when class size reduction programs are well-designed and implemented in the primary grades (K-3), student achievement rises as class size drops." The famous randomised experiment Project Star in the US State of Tennessee concluded that "students placed in smaller classrooms performed better than their peers in larger classrooms across all grade levels tested and across all geographic regions".

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And I note that Project Star, while not perfect, meets the basic gold standard for research, namely a controlled, randomised experiment.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: A University of Glasgow study by Valerie Wilson for the Institute of Education Sciences, the research arm of the US Department of Education, concluded that class size reduction does increase student achievement, especially among those who most need it.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In a 2003 Review of Educational Research article, Finn, Pannozzo and Achilles cited evidence for the visibility principle − students in small classes experienced increased encouragement to participate as they may be called upon more frequently to answer questions or to participate in a class activity.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: There are many other studies that have arrived at similar conclusions, too numerous to mention here.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: These skills to do with communication, confidence and self-mastery are needed for competitiveness in the 21st century and may lead to economic benefits that would justify the additional investment.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: A scholarly article by John Johnston of Memphis State University using STAR data also found that students in smaller classes were more willing to take risks, less inhibited, less afraid of being wrong, volunteered to answer questions more, felt safe with their ideas; were more curious, enthusiastic and eager to participate versus those in regular sized classes.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In a 2015 article in the British Educational Research Journal, Harfitt and Tsui found evidence for smaller class sizes being linked to higher frequency of volunteered responses and greater interactions with teachers via asking questions or clarifications, which relate to communication and confidence.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In a US National Bureau of Economic Research article in 2008, Dee and West found links between smaller classes and non-cognitive skills that are highly predictive of long-term education and labour-market outcomes.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Thirdly, as a result of the factors above, smaller classes may reduce our dependence on Singapore's massive private tuition industry.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In the tuition industry, much smaller classes are near-universal.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Less tuition and less remedial classes as a result of more effective teaching in smaller classes would free up children's time to explore and develop other aspects of character, learning and skills.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Class size reduction also has an egalitarian dimension.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Better-off students can always afford to cultivate soft skills and content mastery through private tuition, enrichment classes or parental coaching.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Smaller classes may help level the playing field and enhance equality of opportunity for students from disadvantaged backgrounds − which, in turn, may crucially unleash talent from disadvantaged families, the kind of talent that our economy needs.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: An analysis of multiple studies by David Zyngier of Monash University, drawing on data from several countries and reviewing 112 papers over 35 years, concluded that "smaller class sizes in the first four years of school can have an important and lasting impact on student achievement, especially for children from culturally, linguistically and economically disenfranchised communities".

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In a previous exchange I had in this House with Minister Ng Chee Meng relating to class size, the Minister cited that smaller class sizes could be found in subject-based banded classes and remedial classes and classes under the Learning Support Programme, though it was revealed in reply to my previous written Parliamentary Question that the size of remedial classes is not tracked by MOE.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, remedial classes with smaller class sizes do not fully address the arguments I have shared here for two reasons.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: There is evidence that self-confidence or self-esteem affects academic performance, potentially creating a vicious cycle, for example, a 2011 study by Booth and Gerard.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: There is also some evidence that smaller class sizes may increase teacher retention.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Continuity matters to learning outcomes because a teacher who knows his or her students deeply and builds rapport with them will be a more effective teacher.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: A 2008 paper by Price and Terry of the National Council of Professors of Educational Administration in the USA found evidence of a link between smaller classes and a higher level of teacher satisfaction because smaller classes allowed for more and better enrichment activities.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The same study also found evidence that smaller classes may reduce teacher attrition.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Using data from the SAGE study, Molnar, Smith and Zahorik, in a 1999 paper, found evidence for a link between smaller classes and fewer discipline problems.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The 2015 Harfitt study found that teachers linked smaller class size to having more freedom to plan and interact, less trial-and-error, less worry over deadlines for marking and homework preparation, improved classroom management and the ability to know their pupils better.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Opponents of class size as a driver of outcomes often cite the work of John Hattie, an Australian researcher, which some have cited as disproving that class size makes a difference.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This work has been criticised by other researchers, notably Ivan Snook from Massey University.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The criticism centres on the problems associated with Hattie's methodology of synthesising a whole range of meta-studies on a simple quantitative scale.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: No control separates good research from bad and more robust gold standard research, like the Tennessee STAR study, from other kinds of studies.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Also, Hattie's work focuses on quantifiable academic performance, not attributes like non-cognitive skills and attitudes where evidence suggests smaller classes are of significant benefit.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The same objection applies to the work of Wormann and West in 2002 which, while it claims zero class size effect in Singapore, relies mainly on historical data from the TIMSS database on maths scores, is not a randomised experiment nor measures other subjects, let alone non-cognitive skills.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It should also be noted that class size is not the same as student-teacher ratio (STR).

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In terms of STR, the gap between Singapore and other countries may not be as large.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, favourable STRs may be consistent with unfavourable class sizes, depending on how much of a teacher's time is spent teaching, how many classes are held and so on.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If the trial is positive, we should move towards a universal form class size of 20-25 as a goal.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Twenty to 25 seems a good balance point between what is desirable and what is feasible in respect of cost and availability of teachers.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is a little above the 2010 OECD average.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, the cost implications of this suggestion should be less of an issue with current declining enrolments, which give us an opportunity to redeploy teachers to smaller classes.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And I can think of few other more important national priorities in long-term spending than getting our education right.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Education is really one of the key, if not the key competitive success factor for our economy going forward because it potentially creates pathways to innovation, productivity and entrepreneurship.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If incremental cost is an issue, let us debate this with the benefit of the numbers so that potential trade-offs can be explored in a concrete manner.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And the speed at which we move towards this goal can thus be calibrated accordingly.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Such a trial should be designed and supervised by an independent academic panel of recognised professionals and the results published for scrutiny.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The change should be used as a pivot to revamp our pedagogy in schools, to shift it towards more classroom participation designed to engender non-cognitive skills and attributes, as well as to level up across students from different socio-economic and family backgrounds.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The speed at which we can move towards this goal will depend on fiscal resources.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But such a change should reduce the need for remedial classes, which may generate cost savings.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This change may also produce benefits in terms of teacher satisfaction, which may be linked to productivity, effectiveness and reduced attrition of teachers, which has cost benefits, too.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Our economy's competitiveness as a developed country in the 21st century, amidst all the disruption from artificial intelligence and other factors that will unfold, hinges on the quality of our human resources.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We need to churn out future entrepreneurs and disruptors.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Let us not shirk from giving all students the kind of benefits of small class sizes that Gifted Education Programme students now enjoy and that established academic research has demonstrated.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And not by way of remedial classes that have their own down-sides and side effects.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Let us not shirk from making the changes needed to turn Singapore's future classrooms into incubators of innovation and catalysts for equality of opportunity.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: We stay abreast of good educational practices and developments in other countries, and constantly review how we can take ideas and adapt them to our context, including ideas that have been discussed in this House by my esteemed colleagues, including Ms Denise Phua.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: My Ministry has already embarked on this journey to nurture future-ready and responsible learners, bringing the future classroom into reality today.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: I will share briefly about our holistic approach in three areas: Learners; Learning Spaces, in which technologies are embedded; and Teachers.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: It is teachers and how they teach that make the critical difference, not class sizes.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: First, maximising the potential of every child starts with the Learner.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Our curriculum has shifted to focus more on 21st Century Competencies, such as Critical and Inventive Thinking, that enable our students to solve real-world problems creatively; and Collaboration and Communication skills that enable them to work effectively in teams.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Earlier this year, I spoke about the importance of nurturing the joy of learning in our children.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: This is so that they can discover their interests and passions.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: This intrinsic motivation is key to lifelong learning and success.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: I stressed the importance of developing an entrepreneurial dare so that our children will have the resilience, adaptability and enterprising spirit to apply their learning to real-world contexts and pursue their passions.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: These are key aspects of a holistic education, not just simply class sizes.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Taken together, these fundamental dispositions, attitudes and skills will help our students thrive in an uncertain and complex world.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: We will continue to enhance our focus on nurturing these dispositions, while moving away from an over-emphasis on academic grades.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: We are already evolving our Learning Spaces beyond the classroom to provide for a more authentic learning experience.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: To prepare our children for the future, it is not just about class sizes, but how we get them to apply their learning; because Applied Learning connects what they learn in the classroom with real-world contexts, be it in the STEM arena, the Arts or the Humanities domain.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: It combines content mastery with a more applied and practice-oriented approach to learning.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Using their knowledge and skills, students can experiment, investigate and develop innovative ideas and solutions to real-world problems.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Through hands-on experience and exposure, they can better discover their strengths and interests, as well as their future education and career pathways.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: The "Lab on Wheels", a bus that travels from school to school, allows students to tinker with modern technologies, such as 3D printers, drones and other fun stuff.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: How do you calibrate class sizes in such activities?

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: We should not fixate on a single dimension of success in education.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Coding and technology are just two examples of ALPs that are offered in our schools.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Many of the ALPs in STEM areas, such as Health Science, Transport and Communication, and Robotics are very welcome.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: There are also non-STEM areas, such as in the Languages, Humanities, Business and Entrepreneurship.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: In line with the chosen ALP focus, schools design and deliver activities to expose students to these new areas and fuel their passion for learning, in and outside the classroom.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Many of the ALPs have been developed with relevant industry partners, Government agencies and even Institutes of Higher Learning (IHLs).

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Students with keen STEM interest can develop their interests through these programmes or relevant Co-Curricular Activities (CCAs).

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Again, how do we measure these programmes through class sizes?

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Upper Secondary students can go one step further.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: They can take up Advanced Elective Modules or Applied Subjects.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Examples of these include Computing and Electronics for the Express and Normal (Academic) courses and Mobile Robotics and Smart Electrical Technology for the Normal (Technical) courses.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Again, this is not in the era where Mr Perera and I grew up where they are all standardised – 40 in a class.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Feedback from students who took these modules or subjects have been very positive.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: They enjoyed seeing their learning come alive and were engaged in the process, regardless of which course they are from.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: In addition, we are also redesigning the education experience for students to provide a more customised learning space to help every child realise his potential.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: What I mentioned in ALPs are just one way we do so, to cater to learners with different interests and aptitudes.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Lower Secondary students in the Normal (Academic) and Normal (Technical) courses will be able to take their stronger subject(s) at a higher academic level.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: This, as the Member has mentioned, could be in class sizes of 10, 15 or 20.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: This flexibility allows students to stretch themselves in their areas of strength and build a strong academic foundation.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Such a foundation will position them well to harness future technologies and future learning so that they can thrive.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: For example, many of the skills needed are already developed today in our classrooms, regardless of class sizes.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: We are also making more learning resources available to students on the online space to enable them to pursue their interests in a self-directed manner.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: When we look at the classrooms of the future, on the online space, how do we define class size?

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Riding on this technology and with these resources, students can access additional material according to their interest, and at their own pace anytime, anywhere.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: This is learning in the future classroom, beyond class sizes.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Third, competent and dedicated teachers remain key to our students' learning.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: We invest in our teachers because teacher quality is critical to improving student outcomes.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: This is most decisive, backed by OECD research.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: In spite of the different research that the Member has quoted, these researches are not conclusive.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Instead of reducing class sizes across the board, schools deploy teachers flexibly to keep the class sizes smaller for students who need that extra support.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Pull-out classes, as I informed the Member previously, for levelling-up, can be in smaller classes of six to eight.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: And, as I have said before, too, the form class size is not indicative of the learning support or attention that our students are receiving.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: The future classroom does not look like what it was yesteryear.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Schools already band students into smaller teaching groups based on their learning needs, for example, in the levelling-up programmes and Subject-Based Banding classes that I have mentioned.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: It brings together the shared beliefs of Singapore educators − past and present − and effective practices that lead to engaged and joyful learning across our schools.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng
text: With this common reference point, teachers can innovate their teaching practices to better meet the evolving needs of students today.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng
text: Our teachers also continue to keep themselves current with the latest pedagogy, as well as suitable education technologies.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng
text: Within their schools, they are supported by trained mentors.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng
text: And beyond their schools, they are committed to a range of in-service professional development courses, as well as networked learning communities.
